text:
The three days of travel in Genesis 22 may be read as a kind of suspended sentence; nothing outward happens in them, and yet everything of significance happens. The narrator lingers upon the servants, the wood, the knife, and the fire, and by lingering upon them he names the instruments of the act before the act itself occurs. The story presents obedience and horror together, and never lets either prevail over the other. Faith, in such a narrative, is a structured arrangement; it is no feeling.

When the scene is compared with the earlier promise, the difference between them narrows. The reader has been reminded that Isaac is the child of the covenant, the one through whom the nations are to be blessed; and that promise is now turned into a test. The whole scene turns upon a single word, _hineni_, "here I am," and in this story the language of being present is also the language of loss. Abraham speaks the word three times, once to God, once to Isaac, and once to the angel. Each time it means something different, and each time it costs him more.
